markers.name: TSH
markers.explain: TSH signals the thyroid to produce hormones. High TSH = underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism). The pituitary gland is working overtime to compensate.
markers.note: Subclinical hypothyroidism (T3 and T4 still normal). Elevated TSH tends to raise LDL, lower HDL, and cause fatigue and weight gain; a medication dose review may help.

markers.name: Free T3
markers.explain: Free T3 is the active thyroid hormone driving metabolism. Normal Free T3 with high TSH = subclinical hypothyroidism.
markers.note: Reflects that enough T4 is still converting to T3; this may not hold if TSH keeps rising.

markers.name: Free T4
markers.explain: Free T4 is the storage hormone. The body converts it to active T3 as needed.
markers.note: If this drops below range while TSH rises, it would mark a shift from subclinical to overt hypothyroidism.

markers.name: Total T3
markers.explain: Total T3 measures all triiodothyronine in the blood (both bound and free). Normal Total T3 alongside a high TSH points to subclinical rather than overt hypothyroidism.
markers.note: The thyroid still makes enough active hormone despite the raised TSH.

markers.name: Total T4
markers.explain: Total T4 measures all thyroxine in the blood. The body converts T4 to active T3 as needed. Normal T4 with a high TSH means the thyroid is keeping output up under pituitary pressure.

markers.name: HDL
markers.meta: Target: >40 (ideally >50) | Below range in ALL tests
markers.explain: HDL removes excess cholesterol from arteries. Low HDL is an independent cardiovascular risk factor, especially prevalent in Indians (~66% have low HDL per LAI-2020).
markers.note: Low HDL is driven by hypothyroidism and a likely sedentary routine; regular exercise is the main lever.

markers.name: LDL
markers.explain: LDL deposits cholesterol in artery walls. Primary target for cardiovascular risk reduction per NCEP/LAI guidelines.
markers.note: Hypothyroidism directly raises LDL, so improving TSH could lower it without medication.

markers.name: Triglycerides
markers.explain: Triglycerides are dietary fats. High TG = cardiovascular risk, especially in Indians with atherogenic dyslipidemia (high TG + low HDL + high LDL).
markers.note: Very sensitive to the previous evening's meal; keeping it controlled also normalizes VLDL and the cholesterol ratios.

markers.name: Total Cholesterol
markers.explain: Sum of all cholesterol fractions. A blunt instrument, can mask bad composition (low HDL + high LDL).
markers.note: Total cholesterol alone is misleading here; HDL and the Chol/HDL ratio matter more.

markers.name: VLDL
markers.explain: VLDL carries triglycerides. Calculated as TG/5. High VLDL = high TG being circulated.
markers.note: Tracks triglycerides directly; controlling TG brings VLDL down with it.

markers.name: Chol/HDL Ratio
markers.explain: Better predictor of cardiovascular risk than any single lipid. Reflects the balance of harmful vs. protective cholesterol.
markers.note: Driven by low HDL; raising HDL toward 45 would pull the ratio near 4.0 and materially lower cardiovascular risk.

markers.name: Vitamin D
markers.explain: Vitamin D supports bone health, immune function, and mood. Deficiency is epidemic in India despite sunny climate (indoor work, pollution, skin pigmentation).
markers.note: Supplementation worked; a maintenance dose (about 1000 IU/day) keeps it up.

markers.name: Vitamin B12
markers.explain: B12 is essential for nerve function and blood cell production. Deficiency causes fatigue, tingling, cognitive issues. Common in Indian vegetarian diets.
markers.note: Oral B12 maintains the level; it falls again if stopped.

markers.name: Sodium
markers.explain: Sodium maintains fluid balance and nerve function. Low sodium (hyponatremia) causes headaches, fatigue, confusion. Hypothyroidism is a known cause.
markers.note: A low reading can reflect hypothyroidism or over-hydration before the test; worth monitoring.

markers.name: Potassium
markers.explain: Critical for heart rhythm and muscle function.

markers.name: HbA1c
markers.explain: Reflects average blood sugar over 2-3 months. Gold standard for diabetes screening.

markers.name: Fasting Glucose
markers.explain: Snapshot of current blood sugar after overnight fast.

markers.name: Hemoglobin
markers.explain: Oxygen-carrying protein in blood. Low = anemia.

markers.name: Platelets
markers.explain: Blood clotting cells.

markers.name: WBC
markers.explain: Immune cells fighting infection.

markers.name: ESR
markers.explain: Non-specific inflammation marker.
markers.note: Occasional mild spikes can happen without chronic inflammation.

markers.name: AST/SGOT
markers.explain: Liver enzyme. Elevated = liver stress/damage.

markers.name: ALT/SGPT
markers.explain: Liver-specific enzyme. More sensitive than AST for liver issues.

markers.name: Bilirubin Total
markers.explain: Byproduct of red blood cell breakdown. High = liver/gallbladder issues.
markers.note: A slow rise that stays within range can indicate benign Gilbert's syndrome; worth watching.

markers.name: Albumin
markers.explain: Main liver-produced protein. Reflects nutrition and liver function.

markers.name: Creatinine
markers.explain: Muscle waste product filtered by kidneys. Stable creatinine = stable kidney function.

markers.name: Uric Acid
markers.explain: From purine metabolism. High = gout risk, kidney stones. Affected by diet, hydration, and hypothyroidism.
markers.note: Addressable with hydration (about 3 L/day) and lower purine intake; hypothyroidism also contributes.

markers.name: eGFR
markers.explain: Kidney filtration rate. >90 = normal. Naturally declines ~1/year after 40.

markers.name: Urea
markers.explain: Protein breakdown product. High = kidney issues or high protein diet.
markers.note: A rise within range usually reflects higher protein intake; creatinine and eGFR confirm kidney function is fine.

notes.antiTPO: NEGATIVE (<3.00 IU/mL), not Hashimoto's. Natural thyroid management is viable.
